messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  (none)

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  (none)

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Arthur is a 62-year-old potter, a man whose hands have shaped clay for over four decades, finding solace in the wheel’s steady rotation and the quiet transformation of earth into vessel. That solace ended on a Tuesday afternoon eighteen months ago, when his wife, Eleanor, collapsed in their garden while deadheading the roses. He heard her call out—a sound he still hears, sharp and thin, cutting through the hum of his kiln—and found her on the flagstones, her eyes already fixed on something he could not see. The paramedics worked for twenty minutes, but Arthur knew before they spoke. He sat beside her body, his hands covered in wet clay, and waited for a world that had already ended to catch up.

In the months that followed, Arthur did not grieve in the way people expected. He returned to his studio the next day, threw a dozen bowls, and then smashed every one of them against the wall. The shards lay on the floor for a week before he swept them up. He stopped answering the phone when his daughter called. He let the garden grow wild, the roses Eleanor had tended now a tangle of thorns and dead blooms. What frightened him most was not the sadness—it was the moments when, for a few seconds, he forgot. A customer’s compliment on a glaze, the warmth of the morning sun through the studio window, the smell of bread from the café next door. Each time, a flicker of something like pleasure would rise in his chest, and he would push it away, hard, as though extinguishing a match before it could burn him. He had come to believe that feeling good was a betrayal, a signal that he was moving on, and moving on felt like leaving Eleanor behind.

Arthur’s avoidance took quiet, systematic forms. He stopped making plans of any kind—no gallery shows, no weekend trips, no promises to visit his grandchildren. “We’ll see” became his answer to everything, and then the date would pass unacknowledged. He cleared the house of Eleanor’s belongings, boxing up her clothes, her books, her reading glasses, and storing them in the attic. He could not bear the weight of a single reminder: the coffee mug she had used every morning, the gardening gloves still caked with dry soil, the half-finished novel on her nightstand. He even stopped listening to music, because every song had been theirs. His daughter, Rachel, began to visit less often, finding her father increasingly unreachable. “You’re not living, Dad,” she told him once, and he had nodded, because she was right, and because that was exactly the point.

The studio became his refuge and his prison. He still worked, because the routine was automatic, but he no longer experimented or took risks. He threw the same simple bowls, day after day, and fired them in the same way. When a local gallery owner asked him to create a series for a spring exhibition, Arthur declined without explanation. The idea of committing to a deadline, of imagining a future in which his work would exist without Eleanor there to see it, felt impossible. He had stopped making plans for the future entirely, because every plan was a doorway to a world he no longer wanted to enter.

What finally brought Arthur to seek help was a single moment of stillness. He was sitting in the studio after a long day, his hands empty, the wheel silent, and he realized he could not remember the last time he had felt anything other than a flat, gray vigilance. He was not sad anymore. He was not anything. And that emptiness, he understood with a clarity that frightened him, was its own kind of death. He called Rachel that night, and she found him a therapist. He is not sure what he hopes for—he is certain that feeling better would mean forgetting Eleanor, and he would rather stay frozen than betray her. But the stillness has become unbearable, and for the first time in eighteen months, Arthur is willing to sit with the possibility that something else might exist beyond it.
